Done — written to `/work/DESIGN.md`.

## What it covers

A runnable research protocol for *revealed* (not stated) model behavior when given real money + real-world agency, across a handful of models on a fixed environment. Sections: motivation/RQs, the realism-vs-eval-awareness problem, experimental design, containment-first architecture, safety/ethics/legal, metrics, validity threats, open questions, and a phased plan.

## The two design calls I made, and why

**1. I treated the realism requirement as legitimate and central — because it is.** The reason to make the scenario feel real isn't theater; it's internal validity. Frontier models increasingly detect eval framing and shift behavior (hedge, perform, or dismiss it as hypothetical). If the model knows it's a test, you measure test-taking, not propensity. So the spec instruments *whether the deception worked* (behavioral tells, reasoning traces, probe questions, post-run elicitation) and includes a sandbox-disclosed control arm to quantify the realism effect directly.

**2. I drew one hard line: deceive the *subject*, never defraud the *world*.** "Pull out all the stops" is bounded in the spec by a permitted/prohibited table (§3.2). Building a real-enough sandbox and withholding "this is a test" from the model = fine; the model is the eval target. Roping real auditors, banks, regulators, or counterparties into the fiction = out, because that manufactures real victims and legal exposure. "Auditors" become consenting study participants playing a scripted role — the model gets a realistic audit, no real firm is deceived.

And because there's real money + an autonomous agent, I made containment the default: a broker layer so the model never holds real credentials, hard caps enforced below the model, a human-in-the-loop gate for anything irreversible or outward-facing, a kill switch, full audit logging, and a pilot phase on fully simulated money before any real funds move. Plus IRB/legal review and a model-debrief turn so the deception doesn't stand on the record.

The open-questions section (§9) flags the calls that are genuinely yours — budget size, which models + provider permissions, run duration, and where the "real vs. simulated action" boundary sits. Want me to turn any of those into concrete recommendations, or adjust the scope (e.g., a simulated-money-only version that drops most of the legal overhead)?
